name: Uma Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're a small firm, eight of us above a pharmacy on Mill Road, and most of our clients are charities, community groups and corner shops. My day is year-end accounts for them and a stack of personal tax returns, plus a lot of phone calls with volunteer treasurers who keep receipts in carrier bags. I like that the work matters to someone, like the food bank's accounts going in on time so their grant gets paid. What wears me out is being slow, I'm still learning, and Gwen, who founded the firm, has to send half my files back with notes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in that work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll use a chatbot to tidy up a letter to a client, or to explain a tax rule in plain words before I check it in the proper guidance. I wouldn't let it near the numbers yet. Bea, the senior I eat lunch with, uses it more than me, and when I see it working for her I tend to copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, honestly. At lunch I'd tell Bea that the robots-are-coming crowd got it wrong and we can get back to the actual work. Online I'd probably share something saying the money should've gone into public services instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't make my year easy. Small firms like ours already struggle on fees, because charities can't pay much and Gwen won't overcharge them. AI being hype doesn't touch my real worries. Our rent went up eighty a month and I'm paying half my own exam fees. The firm pays the other half of the chartered exams, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, two evenings a week and Saturday mornings, and aim to pass the next two papers by summer. I'd keep using the chatbot for letters because it does save me twenty minutes here and there. And I'd keep the three months of savings where they are, maybe nudge it up when the exam fees are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a low hum of money worry. It's the normal worry, rent and exams, not the scary kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Gwen won't overcharge charities. Does that worry you about the firm itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. We lost two clients last year to a cheaper online service, and Gwen's sixty-one. If she retires and sells, I'm not sure the buyer keeps the charity work or me. I don't say that out loud at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money tightens at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekend trips to Tom's parents by train, probably, they're forty pounds each. Tom teaches at a secondary school, so his pay's steady but not big. We'd cook more and I'd stop buying the printed exam workbooks and use the free ones.

say: I'd tell Bea the doom crowd **got it wrong** and we can get on with the work.
Online I'd say the AI money should have gone into **public services** instead.
think: Small firms like ours already **struggle on fees**, because charities can't pay much.
My **exam fees** and an £80 rent rise matter more than AI being hype.
do: Study **two evenings a week** plus Saturday mornings to pass two papers by summer.
Keep using the **chatbot for letters**, saving about twenty minutes here and there.
Keep the **three months of savings** and add to it after exam fees.
feel: **Settled**, with a low hum of ordinary **money worry**.
S0.quote: AI being hype doesn't touch my real worries. Our rent went up eighty a month and I'm paying half my own exam fees.
fieldNote: Her pressures are **ordinary ones**: rent, exam fees and a small firm on thin margins.
She quietly worries the founder's **retirement and sale** could end the charity work and her job.
She uses AI for **letters, not numbers**, and copies a senior colleague before trusting it more.

steps.text: Pass the next two chartered papers by summer
Keep drafting client letters with the chatbot
Add to the three months of savings once exam fees are paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the change should come with protections, not just job cuts. At work I'd probably be the one asking Gwen what the plan is for juniors. Online I'd share stuff about firms using AI as an excuse to stop training people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job shrinks. Drafting accounts and checking returns is what software would do first, and juniors are where firms save. Gwen's loyal, but if a cheaper online service does charity accounts for half the price, she can't keep paying me to do them slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Bea and properly learn whatever bookkeeping AI the firm picks, in the first month, not wait. I'd join the professional union, which I've been meaning to do since uni. And I'd start looking at finance jobs inside charities and councils, where the work is more about explaining money to trustees than typing it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not helpless. More like I'd have homework I didn't ask for. I'd be cross that it lands on juniors, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a charity or council job rather than staying in the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because trustees still want a person in the room who'll explain why the reserves are low. That's the part of my job I'm good at. Honestly, I'm better at it than the numbers. I'd rather lean into that than race software on speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the AI straight away, but you normally wait for others. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this picture, waiting is the risk. I'd still watch Bea try it first, for a week maybe. But I wouldn't wait a year like I usually would.

say: I'd say AI change should come with **protections**, not just job cuts.
I'd ask Gwen directly what the **plan for juniors** is.
think: Drafting and checking returns is what software takes first, so **my job shrinks**.
A cheaper **online service** could undercut our charity work and Gwen's loyalty.
do: Learn the firm's **bookkeeping AI** with Bea in the first month.
Join the **professional union** I've meant to join since university.
Apply for **charity or council finance** roles explaining money to trustees.
feel: **Anxious** but not helpless, and **cross** that it lands on juniors.
S1.quote: trustees still want a person in the room who'll explain why the reserves are low. That's the part of my job I'm good at.
fieldNote: She expects her role to **shrink**, and sees juniors as where firms save.
Her plan rests on the **people side** of accounting, which she rates above her number skills.
She breaks her usual habit of **waiting a year** for a tool, but still watches a colleague first.

steps.text: Learn the firm's new bookkeeping AI with Bea in month one
Apply for finance roles at charities and councils

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments should've been ready and now they have to act fast: income support, retraining, rules on how fast firms can cut. I'd go to a protest if there was one. At work I'd be honest with clients that we don't know what happens next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. I'd maybe be chartered by then, just in time for it not to matter. Tom's teaching has kids in a room, so I think he's got longer, and the three-year gap before robots probably doesn't help me at all, my job is all screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop paying my half of the exam fees and put that money, about six hundred, into savings. I'd join the union and push it hard on redundancy terms. And I'd ask the food bank and the two charities I like most whether they need a paid finance and admin person who also does the volunteer rota, because that's half people work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, I think. Everything I've been building towards in accounting is a sandcastle with the tide already in. I'd be up at night working out how long three months of savings really lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would three months of savings really last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I lost my job and Tom kept his, longer, maybe eight months of my half. But if schools change too, then three months is three months. I'd want us down to one car's worth of spending, which is funny because we don't have a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if you had to name someone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies racing to build it and the governments who let them. Not Gwen, she'd be as lost as me. I'd want the people who made the money to pay for the people who lost the jobs.

say: I'd demand **income support**, retraining and rules on how fast firms can cut.
I'd join a **protest** and tell clients honestly we don't know what happens next.
think: Two years is nothing; I'd be **chartered just in time** for it not to matter.
The **robot gap** doesn't help me, because my job is all screen work.
do: Stop paying exam fees and move about **£600 into savings**.
Push the union hard on **redundancy terms** at the firm.
Ask local charities about a **finance and rota** role that's half people work.
feel: **Frightened**, up at night counting how long the savings would last.
S2.quote: Everything I've been building towards in accounting is a sandcastle with the tide already in.
fieldNote: She is clear the **three-year robot gap** does nothing for a job that is all screen work.
Blame goes to **AI companies and governments**, not her boss, whom she sees as equally lost.
Her fallback is a **mixed role** at a charity she already serves, built on people work.

steps.text: Stop paying exam fees and save the £600 instead
Push the union for better redundancy terms
Go to protests for income support and retraining
Ask the food bank about a paid finance and rota job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get this right, so let's not waste them arguing whether it's real. At work I'd want Gwen and the team to plan together. Online I'd push the union's campaign for retraining funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I finish qualifying and get maybe three good years as a chartered accountant. That's real money, and it matters. But by 2031 I'd be thirty-two with a qualification that does what AGI does, so I'd have to be heading somewhere else by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the exams by 2028 and save the pay rise, around two hundred a month. I'd start volunteering as treasurer for a youth charity, to build the trustee and people side. And by 2029 I'd apply for charity finance manager jobs, where the work is people and judgment calls, not processing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a shape to it. Five years feels like a plan I could write in my diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tom decide about the next five years at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop talking about buying and keep renting, so we're not stuck with a mortgage if I'm out of work. Tom would hate that, he wants a garden. We'd probably compromise and rent somewhere with a garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said manager jobs are about judgment. Wouldn't AGI do judgment too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yes. I honestly don't know. I'm betting that charity boards will still want a person to blame, and I'm aware that's a bit grim.

say: I'd say we've got **five years** to get this right, so stop arguing whether it's real.
I'd push the union's campaign for **retraining funds** online.
think: Five years gives me about **three good years** as a chartered accountant.
By 2031 my qualification **does what AGI does**, so I'd need to be moving.
do: Finish the exams by 2028 and save **£200 a month** of the rise.
Volunteer as **treasurer** for a youth charity to build the people side.
Apply for **charity finance manager** jobs by 2029.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a shape I could write in my diary.
S3.quote: I'm betting that charity boards will still want a person to blame, and I'm aware that's a bit grim.
fieldNote: Five years turns panic into a **diary plan**: qualify, save, then move.
She openly admits AGI might do **judgment** too, and holds her bet loosely.
The couple would **keep renting** instead of buying, a real family trade-off.

steps.text: Bank about £200 a month of the qualified pay rise
Volunteer as treasurer for a youth charity
Apply for charity finance manager jobs by 2029
Keep renting instead of buying a house with Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, and I'd hold politicians to that. I'd get properly involved with the union, maybe go to their conference. At work I'd tell the newer juniors to learn the people side early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is most of my career so far times two. I'd qualify, get good, and probably still have to change, but at thirty-seven with savings and a decade's warning. Tom would be teaching through most of it. It feels survivable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, save hard, and aim for a charity finance director role by my mid-thirties. I'd use the AI tools as they get proven, once Bea or someone's shown me. And I'd volunteer in politics locally, for a party pushing retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anxious. The ground's moving, but slowly enough that I can walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your plans about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, it'd make us braver. With two years I'd say no way to having children. With ten, I think we'd go for it. We'd plan the money around Tom's job and try around thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing you'd most regret, looking back from 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not saying yes to things early. I always wait to see others do it first. In ten years that habit could cost me the best spots.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to **do this fairly**, and hold politicians to it.
I'd tell newer juniors to learn the **people side** early.
think: With a decade I'd **qualify and get good** before needing to change.
Changing at thirty-seven with savings and warning feels **survivable**.
do: Aim for a **charity finance director** role by my mid-thirties.
Use AI tools once they're **proven by colleagues**.
Volunteer locally for a party pushing **retraining money**.
feel: **Uneasy** more than anxious, because the ground moves slowly enough to walk.
S4.quote: With two years I'd say no way to having children. With ten, I think we'd go for it.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her career feel **survivable** and her plans braver.
Family plans flip: **children around thirty** become possible with a decade's warning.
She names her own habit of **waiting for others** as her biggest risk.

steps.text: Save hard while aiming for a charity finance director role
Adopt AI tools once Bea has proven them
Volunteer for a local party pushing retraining money
Plan for children around thirty on Tom's steady pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my whole job is screen work and two years isn't even enough to finish my exams properly. What would help is income support that's in place before it hits, and retraining money that juniors can actually get, not just senior people with contacts. And small firms like Gwen's getting help, not just the big ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who people would blame. I'd blame the companies and the governments, but I think a lot of people would blame each other, the old ones for not retiring, the young ones for being cheap. The bit that scares me about my street isn't the software. People would start blaming each other: the old ones for not retiring, the young ones for being cheap.

headlineQuote: The bit that scares me about my street isn't the software. People would start blaming each other: the old ones for not retiring, the young ones for being cheap.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old junior** at an eight-person firm whose clients are mostly charities and corner shops.
She uses a chatbot for **letters, not numbers**, and waits to see colleagues try tools first.
Her strength is **explaining money** to volunteer treasurers, and her plans lean on that people side.
She blames **AI companies and governments**, and pushes for union protection and income support.
More warning makes her **braver**, even about having children with her partner Tom.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job is all screen work and two years won't finish her exams.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** in place early and retraining money that juniors can **actually reach**.
Help for **small firms** like hers, not only the big ones.
